name: Tripeptide-29
lead: Tripeptide-29 is a short peptide made of three amino acids, glycine, proline and hydroxyproline (Gly-Pro-Hyp), which is the repeating unit of collagen. It is used in firming and anti-aging skincare, added to creams, serums and neck products, with the aim of making skin look firmer, smoother and more resilient. Collagen loss and fragmentation are central to how aging skin sags and wrinkles, which is why collagen-fragment ingredients are marketed for appearance.

It belongs to the family of cosmetic peptides sometimes called matrikines or signal peptides, which are fragments of structural proteins that suppliers say prompt skin cells to make new collagen. Another cosmetic peptide in this family, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), launched in 2000 [2]. In the United States such products are regulated as cosmetics, and the FDA says US law does not recognise cosmeceuticals as a category [1].

Published human trials on topical tripeptide-29 itself are not available. Collagen peptides taken by mouth have been studied in randomised trials for skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkling [3][4][5], and a 2026 review of aesthetic-dermatology peptides concluded that peptide products should be judged individually rather than treated as interchangeable [6].

chain: A collagen-fragment peptide is applied to the skin daily
It is proposed to signal fibroblasts to build collagen
Skin looks firmer and smoother over weeks
angle.text: Tripeptide-29 is applied in a cream or serum to improve the look of skin firmness and fine lines. The firming mechanism comes from supplier descriptions of collagen signalling, while human data come from related oral collagen peptide trials [3][4][5].

paras: Tripeptide-29 is found in firming serums, neck creams and anti-aging moisturizers, sometimes alongside other peptides. Users apply it daily in the hope of firmer-looking skin and softer fine lines.

Matrikine-type peptides are fragments of structural proteins. Suppliers say such fragments signal skin cells that collagen is being broken down and prompt new collagen synthesis. Matrixyl, launched in 2000, is classed in the same family [2].
Collagen-mimetic peptides, whose repeating unit is the Gly-Pro-Hyp motif, have been used since the late 1960s as tools to study collagen and to develop collagen-based biomaterials [7].

Cosmetics in the US do not require pre-market approval of claims, and the FDA states that the law does not recognise cosmeceuticals as a category [1]. Mild irritation is possible on sensitive skin, as with most cosmetic actives.

No studies found on topical tripeptide-29 in humans. Related research concerns collagen peptides taken by mouth. A randomised, placebo-controlled trial published in 2015 reported that daily oral collagen peptides raised skin hydration after eight weeks, and that dermal collagen density increased and fragmentation decreased within four weeks, with effects lasting through twelve weeks. Skin explants showed increased collagen and glycosaminoglycan production [3]. A 2014 randomised trial of specific bioactive collagen peptides reported reduced skin wrinkles and increased dermal matrix synthesis [4], and a 2018 randomised, double-blind trial of low-molecular-weight collagen peptide reported improvements in hydration, elasticity and wrinkling [5]. These trials involve ingested peptides, not creams. A 2024 randomised, double-blinded trial of low-molecular-weight collagen peptide supplementation likewise examined skin health [8].

timeline.event: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4), a related cosmetic signal peptide, is launched. [2]

card.summary: A collagen-fragment peptide in firming creams that people use to make skin look firmer and smoother.

quick.overview:
Tripeptide-29 is a three-amino-acid collagen fragment used in firming skincare. People apply it to help skin look firmer and smoother.

It is found in over-the-counter serums and creams.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers describe it as a signal peptide telling skin cells to make collagen, similar in concept to other matrikine peptides [2].
quick.risks: It is a cosmetic ingredient, so claims are not pre-approved [1]. Mild irritation is possible for sensitive skin.
